title: Solution curves on a slope field with an equilibrium line

stimulus.title: The slope field of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = (y - 2)\cos x</annotation></semantics></math>

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: On the slope field, sketch the solution curve through (0,3)(0, 3) and the solution curve through (0,1)(0, 1).

rubric.point: Curve through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 3)</annotation></semantics></math>: passes through the point, follows the segments and stays above <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>; rising to the right of 0 (leaving the top of the window near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0.77</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 0.77</annotation></semantics></math>, before <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>) and falling to the left of 0 toward a low point near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2.4</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, 2.4\right)</annotation></semantics></math>; drawn across the field.
accept: a curve through (0, 3) consistent with the slope field, extending across the window

rubric.point: Curve through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>: passes through the point, follows the segments and stays below <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>; the mirror image of the first curve in the line <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.
accept: a curve through (0, 1) consistent with the slope field that does not cross y = 2

parts.sample: Through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 3)</annotation></semantics></math>: above <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>; to the right it climbs steeply and leaves the top of the window before <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, then comes back down to about 3.2 at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = 3</annotation></semantics></math>; to the left it falls to a low point near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>2.4</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, 2.4\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and rises a little toward <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = -3</annotation></semantics></math>. Through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>: the mirror image below <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>, highest near <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mo form="prefix" lspace="0" rspace="0">−</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mn>1.6</mn></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(-\frac{\pi}{2}, 1.6\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. Neither crosses the horizontal line <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Write the equation of the constant solution to the differential equation. Explain why the solution curve through (0,1)(0, 1) stays below it.

rubric.point: Constant (equilibrium) solution <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>, because <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>⋅</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = 0 \cdot \cos x = 0</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.

Reason: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math> is itself a solution and solution curves of this equation do not cross, so a curve starting at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 1 < 2</annotation></semantics></math> stays below <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>.
accept: curves cannot cross the equilibrium solution y = 2

the solution through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math> is <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2 - e^{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math> (separation, as in part (d)), and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">e^{\sin x} > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo><</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y < 2</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>

parts.sample: If <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>, then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx} = (2 - 2)\cos x = 0</annotation></semantics></math> for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>, and the derivative of the constant 2 is 0, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math> is a solution. Solution curves of this equation do not cross, so the curve through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>1</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 1)</annotation></semantics></math>, which starts below 2, stays below <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2</annotation></semantics></math>. (A direct check: separating as in part (d) with <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y(0) = 1</annotation></semantics></math> gives <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>−</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y = 2 - e^{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math>, which is less than 2 for every <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x</annotation></semantics></math>.)

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Let y=f(x)y = f(x) be the solution through (0,3)(0, 3). Find the value of xx in (0,π)(0, \pi) at which ff has a relative maximum. Justify your answer.

rubric.point: Justification: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>></mo><mn>2</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) > 2</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{dx}</annotation></semantics></math> has the sign of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos x</annotation></semantics></math>: positive on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(0, \frac{\pi}{2}\right)</annotation></semantics></math> and negative on <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">(</mo><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo>,</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><mo fence="true" stretchy="true">)</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\left(\frac{\pi}{2}, \pi\right)</annotation></semantics></math>. So <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> changes from positive to negative at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>.
accept: dy/dx changes from positive to negative at x = pi/2 because y - 2 > 0

parts.sample: On the curve through <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 3)</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y - 2 > 0</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'(x) = (y - 2)\cos x</annotation></semantics></math> has the sign of <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\cos x</annotation></semantics></math>. It is positive for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mn>0</mn><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">0 < x < \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math> and negative for <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac><mo><</mo><mi>x</mi><mo><</mo><mi>π</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{\pi}{2} < x < \pi</annotation></semantics></math>. Since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0">′</mo></mrow></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f'</annotation></semantics></math> changes from positive to negative at <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>x</mi><mo>=</mo><mfrac><mi>π</mi><mn>2</mn></mfrac></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">x = \frac{\pi}{2}</annotation></semantics></math>, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f</annotation></semantics></math> has a relative maximum there.

parts.label: d
parts.prompt: Find y=f(x)y = f(x), the particular solution with f(0)=3f(0) = 3.

rubric.point: Antiderivatives with a constant: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln|y - 2| = \sin x + C</annotation></semantics></math>.

Uses <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>3</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(0) = 3</annotation></semantics></math> and solves: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 1 = 0 + C</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C = 0</annotation></semantics></math>, and <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = 2 + e^{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math>.

parts.sample: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mfrac><mrow><mi>d</mi><mi>y</mi></mrow><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn></mrow></mfrac><mo>=</mo><mi>cos</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mspace width="0.1667em"></mspace><mi>d</mi><mi>x</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\frac{dy}{y - 2} = \cos x\,dx</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln|y - 2| = \sin x + C</annotation></semantics></math>. At <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>,</mo><mn>3</mn><mo stretchy="false">)</mo></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">(0, 3)</annotation></semantics></math>: <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>ln</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn><mo>+</mo><mi>C</mi></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">\ln 1 = 0 + C</annotation></semantics></math>, so <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>C</mi><mo>=</mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">C = 0</annotation></semantics></math>. Then <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo stretchy="false">|</mo><mo>=</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">|y - 2| = e^{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math>, and since <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>y</mi><mo>−</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>=</mo><mn>1</mn><mo>></mo><mn>0</mn></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">y - 2 = 1 > 0</annotation></semantics></math> at the initial point, <math class="calc-m"><semantics><mrow><mi>f</mi><mo stretchy="false">(</mo><mi>x</mi><mo stretchy="false">)</mo><mo>=</mo><mn>2</mn><mo>+</mo><msup><mi>e</mi><mrow><mi>sin</mi><mo lspace="0" rspace="0.1667em">⁡</mo><mi>x</mi></mrow></msup></mrow><annotation encoding="application/x-tex">f(x) = 2 + e^{\sin x}</annotation></semantics></math>.
